title: ‘I’m Not MAGA,’ Says Man in MAGA Hat
text:
Elon Musk doesn’t know where people got the idea that he’s MAGA. “I’m not MAGA,” he said in an interview yesterday. “I’m not sure what MAGA means.” He went on to describe himself as “ideologically quite moderate” and added, “I don’t think I have, like, any kind of extreme political views.”

 This is the same Elon Musk who last year took the stage at the Conservative Political Action Conference wearing a black MAGA hat and wielding a chainsaw, has opined that “whites are a rapidly dying minority,” called the left “the party of murder,” posted that he loves Donald Trump “as much as a straight man can love another man,” spearheaded the Trump administration’s DOGE initiative, was the largest individual donor to Republicans in the past two elections, and just two weeks ago urged his 240 million–plus followers to “Vote red today!” on the social-media platform that he bought to wage war on the “woke mind virus.”

 The world’s richest man, it seems, has changed his tune. The nearly half a billion dollars that he spent supporting Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms? That was aimed only at ensuring “checks and balances” in government, he said onstage at The New York Times ’ DealBook Summit yesterday. After the historic Democratic landslide, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO is trying to do what corporate executives often do: adjust their politics to align with the party in power. Mark Zuckerberg banned Trump from Facebook after the Capitol riot on January 6, 2021; four years later, he was standing alongside Trump on the inauguration dais. Palantir CEO Alex Karp donated $1 million to a pro-Trump PAC in December 2024; last week, he told Politico that he’s a lifelong Democrat and that Palantir’s products are “essentially progressive.”

 Musk’s conversion might be the least convincing yet. It’s tricky enough for a chameleon like Zuckerberg to mold his politics to the moment; most Republicans didn’t buy him as a dripped-out, flag-waving, mixed-martial-arts fan any more than most Democrats bought Facebook’s “pivot to privacy” in the wake of the Cambridge Analytica data-harvesting scandal . Musk pitching the public on his new persona as a buttoned-down centrist is like Senator Elizabeth Warren starring in a Cybertruck commercial.

 Musk was not always a right-winger. He has said in the past that he voted for Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton, and Joe Biden. His public swerve to the right began during the coronavirus pandemic and fed on his growing resentments about lockdown policies, transgender rights, and the Biden administration’s exclusion of Tesla from a White House event promoting electric vehicles. He moved from California to Texas in 2020, complaining about regulatory burdens, and brought his companies with him.

 After going all-in on the GOP, Musk now figures to be among the top targets for investigation by a Democrat-led Congress. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts posted on Election Day. And Musk’s business empire is in the awkward position of relying on government contracts and regulatory approvals that will be controlled by political leaders whose party and values he has demonized. Nowhere is this problem more acute for Musk than in his adopted home state of Texas, where the Democrats Gina Hinojosa and James Talarico defeated the Republicans he had backed for governor and the Senate, respectively. Both had campaigned against Musk and data centers. (Musk did not respond to a request for comment.)

 In the past, Musk has criticized politicians who publicly challenged him. When Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon called for a billionaire tax in 2021, he replied with typical delicacy: “Why does ur pp look like u just came?” Since the midterms, however, Musk has exercised uncharacteristic restraint, especially with Hinojosa, who will soon have leverage over not only data centers but also a major planned expansion of SpaceX’s Starbase, Musk’s massive Terafab semiconductor project, and the appointment of judges to the state’s business courts. Two days after the election, he shared a post characterizing Hinojosa’s approach to data centers as “reasonable” and praising her as “a political talent.” That same week, Hinojosa requested a pause on the state’s consideration of a major land sale to SpaceX until she takes office, in January. “We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms,” she said in a CNN interview. Yesterday, Musk reiterated his openness to working with Hinojosa, whom he called by her first name. “Based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor,” he said.

 Mockable as Musk’s pivot might be, there’s a strategic logic to it that doesn’t depend on anyone actually believing that he’s sincere. He made the comments at a conference aimed at business insiders, investors, and policy makers. Tesla and SpaceX stocks took a hit from the midterm results, and Musk has a long history of temporarily pulling back from partisanship when he feels that his business interests are vulnerable. Investors probably don’t care as much about Musk’s politics as they care whether he remains capable of making that trade-off when needed. Musk has floated merging SpaceX and Tesla into one conglomerate, which would require approval from shareholders. And then there are the Democratic politicians Musk hopes to appease at least enough to keep his federal contacts and push through key business deals. Here, too, he doesn’t need them to believe in his conversion. He just needs to signal that he’s open to finding some common ground. Many politicians, after all, recognize the value of malleability in service of expediency.

 Musk’s moderation might well prove short-lived if Democrats don’t respond the way he hopes. (After Musk’s comments yesterday, Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona posted on X: “You are still getting a subpoena.”) Regardless, his sudden circumspection suggests that something significant has already shifted: People watch their words only when they fear consequences. For two years, staying on Trump’s good side was a guarantee of protection for Musk, freeing him to say and do whatever else he wanted. That sense of impunity no longer holds.
